Figure S1. Surface wind fields at different hour of day (6am, noon, 6pm, midnight) under high-T (left column), baseline (middle), and stagnation (right column) meteorological scenarios. Arrow represents wind direction, and color indicates wind speed.


<!-- Page 3 -->


Figure S2. Planetary Boundary Layer (PBL) heights at different hour of day (6am, noon, 6pm, midnight) under high-T (left column), baseline (middle), and stagnation (right column) meteorological scenarios.


<!-- Page 4 -->


Figure S3. Surface temperature fields at different hour of day (6am, noon, 6pm, midnight) under high-T (left column), baseline (middle), and stagnation (right column) meteorological scenarios.


<!-- Page 5 -->


Figure S4. Domainwide emission sums of NOx (top panel) and VOC (bottom panel). Anthropoegnic NOx and VOC emissions are colored by source region, and biogenic emissions are colored in black.


<!-- Page 6 -->


Figure S5. Spatial distributions of NOx (left), anthropogenic VOC (middle) and biogenic VOC (right) emissions in year 2012. Major cities in the domain are labeled.


<!-- Page 7 -->


Figure S6. Spatial distributions of simulated 8-hour (10am-6pm) Odd Oxygen (Ox = O3+NO2) concentration inside the San Joaquin Valley. Note that color legends vary for different years.


<!-- Page 8 -->


Figure S7. Breakdown of anthropogenic contributions by source region: San Joaquin Valley (SJV), San Francisco Bay (SFB), Sacramento Valley (SV), and other air basins (e.g., North Central Coast, South Central Coast, Mountain Counties). Results shown are for baseline meteorology.


<!-- Page 9 -->


Figure S8. Spatial distribution of sensitivity to biogenic VOC (BVOC) under varying emission and meteorology scenarios.


<!-- Page 10 -->


Figure S9. Population distribution inside the San Joaquin Valley.


<!-- Page 11 -->


Figure S10. Preferred precursor type to target inside the San Joaquin Valley (SJV). A grid cell is colored in blue if its anthropogenic VOC (AVOC) contribution to SJV Ox outweighs NOx contribution, and colored in orange otherwise. Results shown are for baseline meteorology.


<!-- Page 12 -->


Figure S11. Maps (top row) show where high-T conditions increase sensitivity to NOx (orange), anthropogenic VOC (blue), or both (yellow). Gray-colored portions indicate source areas where sensitivity changes are negligible. Scatter plots (bottom row) compare changes in sensitivity to NOx versus AVOC at grid cell level, when meteorology switches from baseline to high-T.


<!-- Page 13 -->


Figure S12. Baseline versus high-T rankings of all San Joaquin Valley (SJV) grid cells based on their individual NOx (top) and AVOC (bottom) contributions to the SJV Ox receptor. Higher rankings indicate greater effectiveness when targeting these source areas for emission control. Large correlation coefficients reflect strong consistency in optimal source control strategies between baseline and high-T conditions.


<!-- Page 14 -->


Figure S13. Baseline versus stagnation rankings of all San Joaquin Valley (SJV) grid cells based on their individual NOx (top) and AVOC (bottom) contributions to the SJV Ox receptor. Higher rankings indicate greater effectiveness when targeting these source areas for emission control. Small correlation coefficients for NOx reflect limited consistency in optimal source control strategies between baseline and stagnant conditions.
